questions.q: How does the summary distinguish a target audience from a buyer persona?
a: The audience is the market, the persona is the ideal customer
The audience is online, the persona is offline
The audience buys once, the persona buys repeatedly
The audience is broad, the persona is a competitor
questions.why: Lesson 1 says you define the target audience first, then narrow it to a specific ideal customer figure.

questions.q: Which elements make up an attractive business character?
a: A story, an ongoing tale, flaws, and popularity
A logo, a slogan, a colour, and a mascot
A founder, a mission, a budget, and a team
A promise, a price, a guarantee, and a review
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists a good story, a catchy ongoing tale, natural defects, and popularity.

questions.q: Why does the summary say characters beat companies at connecting with people?
a: People relate to flaws and shared struggles
Characters are cheaper to advertise
Companies cannot tell stories
Characters can be changed every season
questions.why: Lesson 2 says a character with human defects and opinions feels familiar and easy to trust.

questions.q: How should a value ladder be structured?
a: From cheap front-end offers up to expensive ones
From expensive offers down to free gifts
With every product priced the same
With a single offer repeated to new audiences
questions.why: Lesson 3 says you attract leads with low-cost or free offers and guide them toward premium ones.

questions.q: What is a sales funnel, according to the summary?
a: A web page version of your value ladder
A list of customers who already bought
An email sequence sent after a purchase
A discount scheme for returning buyers
questions.why: Lesson 3 defines the funnel as the page representation of the ladder and the path buyers follow.
